title: You are not authorized - missing authorization object in the role
text:
The user gets "You are not authorized to use transaction XXX" or a message that there is no
authorization for a particular activity. They can log on normally, which distinguishes this from a
locked account: the account works, one specific action does not. A background job can fail the same
way when its step user lacks a right that the program checks at runtime.

The role assigned to the user is missing an authorization object, or has the object but not the
field value the program checks - a plant, a company code, an activity. Partially correct
authorisation is the common case and the reason guessing does not work: the user often has the
transaction but not the data behind it.

1. SU53 - have the user run it immediately after the error; it shows the exact failed check while it
   is still i

title: You are not authorized - missing authorization object in the role
text:
action but not the data behind it.

1. SU53 - have the user run it immediately after the error; it shows the exact failed check while it
   is still in their session.
2. STAUTHTRACE - trace all authorization checks for that user when SU53 is not conclusive.
3. ST01 - the older system trace, an alternative when STAUTHTRACE is unavailable.
4. SUIM - find which roles already contain the needed authorization.
5. PFCG - inspect and maintain the role itself.

Add the missing authorization to an appropriate role through the normal approval process, change it
in the development system, and transport it. Keep to least privilege: grant the specific object and
field values the trace showed, not a broad profile. Never resolve this by assigning SAP_ALL, even
temporarily in production - it is the fastes

title: You are not authorized - missing authorization object in the role
text:
ect and
field values the trace showed, not a broad profile. Never resolve this by assigning SAP_ALL, even
temporarily in production - it is the fastest fix and the one that turns a small ticket into an audit
finding.

Role design and approval belong to the security or GRC team. If the user is asking for access they
have no business reason for, that is a conversation for their manager, not a technical fix.

title: Background job status Canceled - read the job log first
text:
SM37 shows the job with status Canceled, usually in red. The job log ends with a message such as
"Job cancelled after system exception ERROR_MESSAGE", or names an ABAP runtime error with
"ABAP/4 processor: <dump name>". Downstream work that depended on the job is missing its data, and
the first sign is often a user asking why a report or interface file is empty this morning.

Several very different things end up looking the same here, which is why the job log must be read
before anything else. A dump inside the program, an error message raised deliberately by the
program, a wrong or deleted variant, a step user that is locked, expired or short of authorisations,
a missing file or unreachable target directory, or an instance restart while the job was running.

1. SM37 - open the Job log bef

title: Background job status Canceled - read the job log first
text:
t of authorisations,
a missing file or unreachable target directory, or an instance restart while the job was running.

1. SM37 - open the Job log before forming any theory; it names the actual failure.
2. ST22 - if the log mentions the ABAP processor, find the dump from the same timestamp.
3. SM21 - the system log around that time, for restarts and resource messages.
4. SU01 - check the step user shown in the job details for lock status and validity.

Repair the underlying cause first: pass the dump to the developer, unlock or renew the step user,
correct the variant, or restore the missing file. Only then repeat the job, normally by copying it
from SM37 rather than editing history. Confirm with the job owner that a rerun is safe before
starting it. Some jobs must not run twice, especiall

title: Background job status Canceled - read the job log first
text:
it
from SM37 rather than editing history. Confirm with the job owner that a rerun is safe before
starting it. Some jobs must not run twice, especially posting and payment runs, because the first
partial run may already have created documents.

Ask the functional owner before any rerun of a job that posts data. Dumps go to the developer. If
the job failed because the instance restarted, that is a Basis question.

- SAP Help Portal - Analyzing the Job Status - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_gbt10/helpdata/en/4b/272d08d1341780e10000000a42189c/content.htm
- Hicron SAP101 - Checking the job log in SM37 - https://hicron.com/sap101/checking-the-job-log-in-sm37

title: Job stuck in Ready or Released - scheduled but never starts
text:
The start time has passed but the job has not run. SM37 shows it as Ready, or as Released and not
moving. There is no job log to read yet and no dump anywhere, because the program never started.
Nothing failed - the job is simply waiting, which is why this looks alarming but is often benign.

The two statuses mean different things and should not be treated alike. Ready means the scheduler
wants to run it but no background work process is available: batch processes are all busy, there are
too few of them, or the job is pinned to a target server that is down. Released means the start
condition itself has not been met: the clock time has not arrived, an awaited event has not been
raised, or a predecessor job has not finished.

1. SM37 - open the job's start condition and target server, and no

title: Job stuck in Ready or Released - scheduled but never starts
text:
ived, an awaited event has not been
raised, or a predecessor job has not finished.

1. SM37 - open the job's start condition and target server, and note which status it is in.
2. SM50 - are the background work processes on this instance all occupied?
3. SM66 - the same question across all instances.
4. SM51 - is the target server named in the job still registered and alive?
5. RZ04 - how many background processes the current operation mode allows.
6. SM62 - for event-driven jobs, whether the awaited event has been raised.

For Ready, free capacity: let long runners finish, or stop one that is holding a process
unnecessarily. If the target server is gone, remove the server restriction so any instance can take
the job. Adjusting the number of background processes, through the profile or the

title: Job stuck in Ready or Released - scheduled but never starts
text:
ver is gone, remove the server restriction so any instance can take
the job. Adjusting the number of background processes, through the profile or the operation mode, is
the structural fix when this recurs. For Released, raise the awaited event or fix the predecessor
job; nothing is wrong with the job itself.

Capacity and operation-mode changes are Basis work. A predecessor that keeps failing belongs to its
own owner, and that is the job to investigate instead.

- SAP Help Portal - Analyzing the Job Status - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_gbt10/helpdata/en/4b/272d08d1341780e10000000a42189c/content.htm
- SAP Help Portal - Work Processes - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/fc/eb2e7d358411d1829f0000e829fbfe/content.htm

title: Object is locked by user - stale lock entries in SM12
text:
A user cannot edit a document and gets a message naming someone else, such as "Purchase order
4500001234 is locked by user JSMITH". Often the named user left hours or days ago. SM12 shows lock
entries older than a day. Sometimes several users are blocked on the same object, and the request
arrives as "please remove this lock" rather than as an error log.

A session ended without releasing its lock, usually because a client crashed or a connection
dropped. A program may hold a lock longer than intended. Importantly, the lock may have been handed
to the update task: when a user saves, the lock is inherited by the update process and is only
released when that update completes. If the update failed or is still queued, the lock is doing its
job and deleting it would be wrong.

1. SM12 - find th

title: Object is locked by user - stale lock entries in SM12
text:
ased when that update completes. If the update failed or is still queued, the lock is doing its
job and deleting it would be wrong.

1. SM12 - find the entry and note the owner, the time it was created, and the table and argument.
2. SM04 - is that user still logged on to this instance?
3. AL08 - the same question across all instances, since the session may live elsewhere.
4. SM13 - the decisive check: does that user have an open or failed update request?
5. SM50 - is a work process still active for that user?

Prefer the gentle route: ask the user to close the transaction or log off, which releases the lock
cleanly. If the session is genuinely dead, end it in SM04. Delete the entry in SM12 only after
confirming that there is no pending or failed update for that user and that the user is n

title: Object is locked by user - stale lock entries in SM12
text:
ly dead, end it in SM04. Delete the entry in SM12 only after
confirming that there is no pending or failed update for that user and that the user is not working,
and record what you deleted and why. Deleting a lock that belongs to a queued update can leave the
document half-posted.

After deleting a lock, ask the functional team to verify the document is consistent. If stale locks
appear daily from the same program, hand it to the developer.

- SAP Help Portal - Example Program: SAP Locking (enqueue and dequeue, SM12) - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/41/7af4c8a79e11d1950f0000e82de14a/content.htm
- SAP Help Portal - Most Important Update Statuses - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_470/helpdata/en/e5/de86ea35cd11d3acb00000e83539c3/content.htm

title: Lock table overflow - the enqueue table is full
text:
Many users suddenly cannot save at once, and the messages mention that a lock could not be set or
that the lock table has overflowed. SM21 contains lock table overflow entries. Short dumps about
failed enqueue operations may appear in the same minutes. The breadth is the signal: a single stale
lock blocks one document, whereas an overflow blocks everyone.

The lock table lives in the enqueue server's shared memory and holds a finite number of entries,
sized by the profile parameter enque/table_size. It fills up when a program or mass job takes an
unusually large number of locks and holds them inside one long transaction, or when the table is
simply sized smaller than the workload needs. A mass update written to lock every record before
committing is the classic cause.

1. SM12 - use Extras

title: Lock table overflow - the enqueue table is full
text:
simply sized smaller than the workload needs. A mass update written to lock every record before
committing is the classic cause.

1. SM12 - use Extras then Statistics to see peak fill and whether an overflow was recorded.
2. SM12 - list current entries and sort by owner to find who holds thousands of them.
3. SM21 - confirm the overflow messages and their exact timing.
4. RZ11 - read the current value of enque/table_size.
5. SM50 - identify the work process and program responsible.

Deal with the cause first: find the job or program taking excessive locks and have it changed to
commit in smaller packages instead of locking everything at once. That is usually a code change, not
a parameter change. Enlarging the lock table in the profile is legitimate once the real demand is
understood, but

title: Lock table overflow - the enqueue table is full
text:
That is usually a code change, not
a parameter change. Enlarging the lock table in the profile is legitimate once the real demand is
understood, but it needs a restart of the enqueue service, so plan it rather than doing it mid-day.

A program locking in bulk goes to the developer with the SM12 statistics attached. Sizing and the
restart are Basis work and need a maintenance window.

- SAP Help Portal - Example Program: SAP Locking (enqueue and dequeue) - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/41/7af4c8a79e11d1950f0000e82de14a/content.htm
- SAP Help Portal - Work Processes, including the enqueue work process - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/fc/eb2e7d358411d1829f0000e829fbfe/content.htm

title: SYSTEM_NO_ROLL / MEMORY_NO_MORE_PAGING - instance is out of shared memory
text:
Short dumps named SYSTEM_NO_ROLL or MEMORY_NO_MORE_PAGING appear in ST22, often several at once and
from different users. Unlike a single large report failing, this pattern usually hits many sessions
in the same few minutes. Users report the system is slow, sessions drop, or saving suddenly fails.
The dumps may name different programs each time, which is the clue that the shortage is
instance-wide rather than caused by one bad program.

The instance could not reserve memory for a user context. Roll area, extended memory or the paging
area is exhausted at that moment. The common reasons are many large user contexts active at the same
time, one session or background job consuming far more memory than expected, or memory parameters
sized smaller than the workload needs. A work process that sw

title: SYSTEM_NO_ROLL / MEMORY_NO_MORE_PAGING - instance is out of shared memory
text:
session or background job consuming far more memory than expected, or memory parameters
sized smaller than the workload needs. A work process that switched to PRIV mode holds its memory
until it finishes, so a few runaway sessions can starve everyone else.

1. ST02 - look at roll area, paging and extended memory, especially the "max used" column rather
   than only the current value.
2. SM50 - check for work processes in PRIV mode and how much memory each holds.
3. SM66 - the same view across all instances, to see whether one instance or all are affected.
4. SM04 - identify the users and sessions holding the largest contexts.
5. ST06 - confirm the host itself still has physical memory and is not swapping.
6. SM21 - read the system log around the same time for related memory messages.

Fin

title: SYSTEM_NO_ROLL / MEMORY_NO_MORE_PAGING - instance is out of shared memory
text:
rm the host itself still has physical memory and is not swapping.
6. SM21 - read the system log around the same time for related memory messages.

Find the session or job consuming abnormal memory and agree with its owner to stop or reschedule it.
Move large reports to background processing and outside peak hours. If PRIV work processes are
stuck, restart them only after checking what they are doing. Review the memory parameters against
the physical memory of the host before changing anything; profile changes need an instance restart,
so plan them. Do not simply raise quotas on a host that is already swapping - that makes the whole
system slower.

Repeated shortages with no single culprit are a sizing question for Basis. If one custom program is
always the cause, hand it to the developer w

title: SYSTEM_NO_ROLL / MEMORY_NO_MORE_PAGING - instance is out of shared memory
text:
wer.

Repeated shortages with no single culprit are a sizing question for Basis. If one custom program is
always the cause, hand it to the developer with the ST02 and SM50 evidence attached.

- SAP Help Portal - Work Processes - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/fc/eb2e7d358411d1829f0000e829fbfe/content.htm
- SAP Help Portal - ABAP Dump Analysis (background) - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_gbt10/helpdata/en/49/1805ac005338a1e10000000a421937/content.htm

title: TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED - internal table cannot be extended (out of memory)
text:
An ABAP program terminates with the runtime error TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED and the short text
"No more storage space available for extending an internal table". It often happens in large
reports, month-end jobs or mass data loads. In a background job, SM37 shows the job as Canceled and
the job log points to the ABAP runtime error. Users may say "the report crashed after running a long time".

The work process could not allocate more memory for an internal table. ABAP memory is allocated
roughly in the order roll area -> extended memory (shared) -> heap memory (private). When the
quotas are used up (parameters such as ztta/roll_extension, abap/heap_area_dia,
abap/heap_area_nondia, abap/heap_area_total) the dump is written. The most common root cause is the
program reading far more data th

title: TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED - internal table cannot be extended (out of memory)
text:
ap/heap_area_dia,
abap/heap_area_nondia, abap/heap_area_total) the dump is written. The most common root cause is the
program reading far more data than intended: a very wide selection, data growth, or code that loads
a whole table without filtering. Less often the instance is simply short of memory at that moment.

1. ST22 - open the dump. Read "Error analysis" (how much memory was requested and already used),
   "Information on where terminated" (program, include, line), "User and Transaction" (user, job name)
   and "Chosen variables" (size of the internal table).
2. ST02 - look at extended memory and heap memory usage and their history: was the instance short
   of memory at that time?
3. RZ11 - check current values of the memory parameters mentioned in the dump.
4. SM37 - if it was a

title: TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED - internal table cannot be extended (out of memory)
text:
as the instance short
   of memory at that time?
3. RZ11 - check current values of the memory parameters mentioned in the dump.
4. SM37 - if it was a job, check the variant/selection and whether data volume grew.
5. SM21 - check the system log around the same time for related memory messages.

First reduce the data volume: narrow the selection, split the run (for example by period or plant),
or schedule it outside peak hours. If the program is custom (Z/Y), ask the developer to process data
in packages and filter in the database. For standard SAP programs, search SAP Notes with the keywords
from "How to correct the error". Increase memory parameters only after analysis, considering the
physical memory of the host; profile changes may need an instance restart.
Do not keep re-running the sam

title: TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED - internal table cannot be extended (out of memory)
text:
ameters only after analysis, considering the
physical memory of the host; profile changes may need an instance restart.
Do not keep re-running the same job unchanged - it will fail again.

Custom program -> ABAP developer (attach the dump, selection and data volume).
Standard program without a matching SAP Note -> SAP Support incident with dump, SM21 and ST02 data.

- SAP Help Portal - ABAP Dump Analysis (background) - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_gbt10/helpdata/en/49/1805ac005338a1e10000000a421937/content.htm
- SAP Community - TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED discussion - https://archive.sap.com/discussions/thread/2107282

title: RFC connection test fails - partner not reached or logon rejected
text:
Short dumps named CALL_FUNCTION_COMMUNICATION_FAILURE or CALL_FUNCTION_SYSTEM_FAILURE appear in
ST22. The connection test in SM59 fails with a message such as "partner not reached", "Name or
password is incorrect", "user is locked", or a timeout during allocate. Interfaces to the named
system stop working, and the error text itself usually tells you whether the problem is the network
or the credentials.

Three groups of cause, and the message distinguishes them. Partner not reached means the target
system or instance is down, the host and instance number in the destination are wrong, or a firewall
blocks the route. Logon failures mean the RFC user's password is wrong, the account is locked, or it
lacks the right authorisations in the target. Gateway rejections mean the target's gateway sec

title: RFC connection test fails - partner not reached or logon rejected
text:
user's password is wrong, the account is locked, or it
lacks the right authorisations in the target. Gateway rejections mean the target's gateway security
rules refuse the connection or the expected registered program is not there.

1. SM59 - run the connection test first, then the authorization or logon test separately; they fail
   for different reasons.
2. SU01 - in the target system, check the RFC user's lock status and validity.
3. SMGW - on the target, look at the gateway monitor for connections, registered programs and
   rejections.
4. SM21 - the system log on both sides around the same time.

Correct whichever layer the message pointed at: fix the host, instance number or service in the
destination; unlock the RFC user and align its password in both the destination and the target

title: RFC connection test fails - partner not reached or logon rejected
text:
ted at: fix the host, instance number or service in the
destination; unlock the RFC user and align its password in both the destination and the target; or
adjust the gateway security configuration. Test again from SM59 after each single change, so you
know which one actually fixed it.

Network routes and firewalls go to the network team. If the target system is down, that is its own
team's incident and not something to fix from this side.

- SAP Help Portal - Displaying, Maintaining and Testing Destinations - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_46c/helpdata/en/22/042638488911d189490000e829fbbd/content.htm
- SAP Learning - Troubleshooting Procedures - https://learning.sap.com/courses/technical-implementation-and-operation-i-of-sap-s-4hana-and-sap-business-suite/troubleshooting-procedures

title: tRFC and qRFC entries stuck - SM58 errors, SMQ1 and SMQ2 queues blocked
text:
Data stops arriving at the receiving system while this system reports no error to users. SM58 lists
entries with error status. SMQ1 or SMQ2 show queues in status SYSFAIL, CPICERR or STOP. Unlike a
failed connection test, the connection may now work again - the entries simply stayed behind after an
earlier outage and nothing has retried them.

The target was briefly unreachable and the calls were parked for retry, or the function module in
the target raised an error so the entry stayed in the queue, or a queue was stopped manually or by a
previous error and never released. For qRFC the order of entries matters: one blocked entry at the
head holds everything behind it, which is why one stuck record can stop an entire interface.

1. SM58 - read the status text of each failed logical unit of w

title: tRFC and qRFC entries stuck - SM58 errors, SMQ1 and SMQ2 queues blocked
text:
lds everything behind it, which is why one stuck record can stop an entire interface.

1. SM58 - read the status text of each failed logical unit of work; it names the real reason.
2. SMQ1 - check outbound queues and their status.
3. SMQ2 - check inbound queues on the receiving side.
4. SM59 - confirm the destination works now, so you know whether the cause has gone.
5. ST22 - look for dumps in the target system at the time the entries failed.

Fix the cause first, then re-execute. SM58 can run a single unit again, and the standard report
RSARFCEX processes many at once. Unlock and activate stopped queues in SMQ1 or SMQ2. With qRFC,
respect the sequence: do not skip a blocked entry to clear the backlog, because later entries may
depend on the one you skipped and the receiving data will be

title: tRFC and qRFC entries stuck - SM58 errors, SMQ1 and SMQ2 queues blocked
text:
he sequence: do not skip a blocked entry to clear the backlog, because later entries may
depend on the one you skipped and the receiving data will be inconsistent.

Errors raised inside the target's function modules belong to the interface or receiving-system team.
Recurring queue stoppages are worth raising as a design question rather than clearing by hand daily.

- SAP Help Portal - Displaying, Maintaining and Testing Destinations - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_46c/helpdata/en/22/042638488911d189490000e829fbbd/content.htm
- Guru99 - SAP monitoring (SM58, SMQ1, SMQ2) - https://www.guru99.com/system-monitoring-performance-checks.html

title: TIME_OUT - dialog step exceeded the maximum run time
text:
A short dump named TIME_OUT with the short text "Time limit exceeded" appears in ST22. The user ran
a report or transaction from the screen and it died after roughly ten minutes. Users describe it as
"it spun for ages and then threw me out". The dump names the program and the line where the system
cut it off, which is wherever it happened to be, not necessarily the slow part.

A dialog work process may only run one step for a limited time, controlled by the profile parameter
rdisp/max_wprun_time, whose traditional default is 600 seconds. Newer kernels may expose this as
rdisp/scheduler/max_runtime, so check the current value rather than assuming. The limit exists to
stop a single user occupying a dialog process indefinitely. The real cause is almost always a slow
database access or a selec

title: TIME_OUT - dialog step exceeded the maximum run time
text:
ing. The limit exists to
stop a single user occupying a dialog process indefinitely. The real cause is almost always a slow
database access or a selection returning far more data than intended, not the limit itself.

1. ST22 - read the dump for the program, the include and the line where it was terminated.
2. SM50 - if the run is still in progress, look at the current action and the table being read.
3. SM66 - the same across instances, useful when several users run the same report.
4. ST05 - take an SQL trace of a smaller run to find the expensive statement.
5. ST12 - a combined ABAP and SQL trace when it is unclear whether time goes to code or database.
6. RZ11 - display the current timeout parameter value and its documentation.

Run the work as a background job: batch work processes are

title: TIME_OUT - dialog step exceeded the maximum run time
text:
or database.
6. RZ11 - display the current timeout parameter value and its documentation.

Run the work as a background job: batch work processes are not subject to this dialog limit, and
this is the normal answer for month-end reports. Narrow the selection so less data is read. Ask the
developer or DBA to improve the statement, add an index or refresh statistics. Raising the timeout
parameter is a last resort because it applies to the whole instance and lets one user hold a dialog
process for longer.

Slow custom code or a missing index goes to the developer or DBA with the trace attached. A standard
SAP program that is slow without explanation is worth searching SAP Notes for.

title: TIME_OUT - dialog step exceeded the maximum run time
text:
tion is worth searching SAP Notes for.

- SAP Help Portal - ICM and dispatcher parameters including rdisp/max_wprun_time - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_snc700_ehp01/helpdata/en/48/6360918c4a31cbe10000000a42189d/content.htm

title: Work processes running too long - no free processes, system feels slow
text:
No dump is written, which is what distinguishes this from TIME_OUT. Instead users report the whole
system is slow or unresponsive. SM50 shows dialog work processes in status Running for a long time,
and few or no processes are free. New logons are slow or rejected. The action column often shows
"Sequential Read" against the same large table for several processes at once.

Heavy work is holding work processes. Typical reasons are a report with no suitable index scanning a
large table, several users starting the same expensive report, database lock waits where sessions
queue behind each other, or the database itself being slow because of its own load or missing
statistics. Because the dispatcher has a fixed number of processes, a handful of long runners is
enough to make the instance look do

title: Work processes running too long - no free processes, system feels slow
text:
n load or missing
statistics. Because the dispatcher has a fixed number of processes, a handful of long runners is
enough to make the instance look down to everyone else.

1. SM66 - the global view first: how many processes, how long, which action, which table.
2. SM50 - drill into one instance for details and the developer trace of a specific process.
3. ST05 - trace SQL for a representative session to find the statement that is slow.
4. ST12 - combined ABAP and SQL trace when the split between code and database is unclear.
5. ST06 - check host CPU, memory and disk, to separate "SAP is busy" from "the host is saturated".
6. ST04 - look at database performance and wait situations.

Identify the owning users and agree to stop or postpone the heavy work. Cancelling a work process is
possible

title: Work processes running too long - no free processes, system feels slow
text:
tabase performance and wait situations.

Identify the owning users and agree to stop or postpone the heavy work. Cancelling a work process is
possible but should be a considered decision, not a reflex, and "cancel without core" is the gentler
option. Move recurring heavy reports to background jobs at quiet times. The durable fix is usually an
index, better statistics, or code that filters in the database rather than in ABAP.

Database waits, missing indexes and statistics go to the DBA. Inefficient custom reports go to the
developer with the trace. If it recurs daily at the same hour, treat it as a capacity question.

text:
Processes - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nw73/helpdata/en/fc/eb2e7d358411d1829f0000e829fbfe/content.htm

title: Transport return code 12 or higher, or an import that never finishes
text:
The import ends with return code 12 or 16, or reports a "tp error", or sits in status running far
longer than such a request should take. The difference from return code 8 is that the request's
content was never really processed: the transport tooling itself could not do its work, so the logs
talk about files and connections rather than about objects and activation.

The problem is outside the request. The tp or R3trans programs could not reach the database, files
in the transport directory are missing or unreadable because cofiles and data files were not copied
or have wrong permissions, the transport filesystem is full, or the import background job RDDIMPDP
is not scheduled so nothing picks the request up. Return codes above 200 are combined values and
need the explainrc utility to decod

title: Transport return code 12 or higher, or an import that never finishes
text:
ound job RDDIMPDP
is not scheduled so nothing picks the request up. Return codes above 200 are combined values and
need the explainrc utility to decode.

1. STMS - open the import monitor and read the tp system log and action log for the request.
2. SM37 - check whether RDDIMPDP is scheduled and running in the target client and in client 000.
3. SM21 - look for database or filesystem messages at the same time.

Repair the environment, then re-import. Restore missing cofiles and data files from the source
system, correct ownership and permissions on the transport directory, or free disk space. If
RDDIMPDP is missing, reschedule it with the standard report RDDNEWPP and confirm it starts picking
up the queue. Only after the tooling works again does re-importing make sense.

This usually needs

title: Transport return code 12 or higher, or an import that never finishes
text:
ndard report RDDNEWPP and confirm it starts picking
up the queue. Only after the tooling works again does re-importing make sense.

This usually needs operating-system access to the transport directory, so it is Basis work and often
needs the platform team as well. Involve the DBA if the logs point at the database connection.

- SAP Help Portal - Return Codes in the Transport Log - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_46c/helpdata/en/57/38e26c4eb711d182bf0000e829fbfe/content.htm

title: Transport import ended with return code 8 - objects did not activate
text:
The STMS import history shows the request in red with return code 8. After the import, a program may
have a syntax error, a table may not be active, or a function module may be reported as missing. The
import did finish - unlike a hanging import - but part of its content did not come across usable.
Users in the target system notice it as a transaction that suddenly dumps.

Some objects in the request could not be imported or activated. The usual reasons are a syntax error
in the transported code, a dependent object that lives in another request which has not been
imported yet, so the import order is wrong, or a table or structure conversion that could not be
performed. Return code 4 is different: it means warnings only, and does not require this procedure.

1. STMS - open the import queue

title: Transport import ended with return code 8 - objects did not activate
text:
hat could not be
performed. Return code 4 is different: it means warnings only, and does not require this procedure.

1. STMS - open the import queue and history, then the logs for the failing request.
2. STMS - inside the log, identify which step returned 8: import, activation, or generation.
3. SE01 - list the objects contained in the request.
4. SE09 - look for sibling requests that should have gone first.
5. SE38 - run a syntax check on the affected program in the target system.
6. SE80 - inspect the object and whether it is active.

If an object depends on something not yet imported, import the missing request and then re-import
this one in the correct order. If the code itself is wrong, it must be corrected in the development
system and released as a new request; do not try to repair

title: Transport import ended with return code 8 - objects did not activate
text:
in the correct order. If the code itself is wrong, it must be corrected in the development
system and released as a new request; do not try to repair objects directly in the target. Check
afterwards that the previously broken objects are active, and tell the affected users once they are.

The developer who owns the request fixes the content. Decisions about import order and whether to
re-import belong with Basis and the release manager together.

- SAP Help Portal - Return Codes in the Transport Log - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_46c/helpdata/en/57/38e26c4eb711d182bf0000e829fbfe/content.htm
- SAP Help Portal - tp Return Codes - https://help.sap.com/saphelp_nwes72/helpdata/en/3a/58c2e9f47611d184850000e8a57770/content.htm

title: Update deactivated - nobody in the system can save
text:
Saving fails across the whole system rather than for one user, and the calls arrive quickly from
everywhere. SM14 shows the update system as deactivated. SM21 carries messages about the update
being switched off. SM13 accumulates requests that are waiting rather than failing. The scope is
what separates this from a single terminated update: everyone is affected at once.

The system deactivates updating by itself when it meets a serious, repeated problem, to avoid
losing data silently. The trigger is usually underneath SAP rather than in it: the database is out
of space, a tablespace is full, the database connection broke, or the filesystem holding the data
filled up. Treating it as an SAP problem and simply reactivating will fail again within minutes.

1. SM14 - confirm the update system s

title: Update deactivated - nobody in the system can save
text:
lding the data
filled up. Treating it as an SAP problem and simply reactivating will fail again within minutes.

1. SM14 - confirm the update system status and when it was deactivated.
2. SM21 - find the first message in the sequence; that one names the real cause.
3. DB02 - check database and tablespace space, and recent growth.
4. SM13 - see how many requests are queued and waiting to be processed.

Fix the underlying problem first - add space, restore the database connection, clear the filesystem.
Only then reactivate updating in SM14. Afterwards work through SM13 and confirm the queued requests
process cleanly, because some may still fail for their own reasons. Reactivating before the cause is
fixed simply repeats the outage and adds more queued work.

Database space and connectivity b

title: Update deactivated - nobody in the system can save
text:
for their own reasons. Reactivating before the cause is
fixed simply repeats the outage and adds more queued work.

Database space and connectivity belong to the DBA, and this is usually their incident rather than
yours. Inform the functional teams that postings between the outage and the fix may need checking.

title: Update was terminated - SM13 entries with status ERR
text:
The user receives an express message in their SAP inbox saying "Update was terminated", usually a
minute or two after saving. SM13 lists one or more update requests with status ERR for that user.
From the user's point of view the save appeared to succeed but the data is not in the system, which
makes this more confusing to them than an outright error on screen.

The user's dialog step finished and handed the database work to the update task, which then failed.
Common reasons are a short dump inside the update function module, data that violates a check only
evaluated at update time, a duplicate key, or a database error such as a full tablespace. Because
the failure happens asynchronously, the dump belongs to the update work process rather than to the
user's session.

1. SM13 - open the fai

title: Update was terminated - SM13 entries with status ERR
text:
ce. Because
the failure happens asynchronously, the dump belongs to the update work process rather than to the
user's session.

1. SM13 - open the failed entry: status, user, time, and the function module that failed.
2. ST22 - find the dump from the same timestamp, which carries the real technical reason.
3. SM21 - the system log, which shows database-level problems around the same time.

Correct the cause before touching the queue. Once it is genuinely fixed, SM13 can repeat the update,
but only do that when you are confident the transaction has not already been posted in part, or you
will create duplicates. Entries that cannot be repaired should be deleted following your local
procedure, and the functional team must then be told to re-enter the business transaction, because
the data is

title: Update was terminated - SM13 entries with status ERR
text:
should be deleted following your local
procedure, and the functional team must then be told to re-enter the business transaction, because
the data is simply missing until they do.

Dumps inside update modules go to the developer. Missing or incomplete business data is a functional
matter. Repeated failures caused by database space belong to the DBA.

title: User is locked - failed logons, administrator lock or expired validity
text:
The user cannot log on and sees a message such as "User is locked. Please notify the person
responsible". The same lock also breaks anything else running under that account: background jobs
whose step user is locked fail, and RFC connections using it stop working. So the first report may
come from a failed job rather than from a person, which is a useful clue that an account, not a
program, is the problem.

Either the system locked the account after too many wrong passwords, counted against the parameter
login/fails_to_user_lock, or an administrator locked it deliberately, or a central user
administration lock applies, or the account's validity period has simply expired. Expired validity
is easy to miss because it is not shown as a lock in the usual sense but has the same effect.

1. SU01

title: User is locked - failed logons, administrator lock or expired validity
text:
ty period has simply expired. Expired validity
is easy to miss because it is not shown as a lock in the usual sense but has the same effect.

1. SU01 - open the user and read the lock status and the logon data, including validity dates and
   user type.
2. SUIM - list locked users, useful when several accounts are affected at once.
3. SM20 - if the security audit log is active, see where the failed logon attempts came from.
4. SM21 - the system log around the same time, as a cross-check.

Verify who is asking before unlocking anything, through an established channel and not just by
email. Then unlock or reset the password in SU01, or use SU10 for several accounts. For a system or
communication account, also correct the stored password wherever it is used, such as in RFC
destinations, other

title: User is locked - failed logons, administrator lock or expired validity
text:
for several accounts. For a system or
communication account, also correct the stored password wherever it is used, such as in RFC
destinations, otherwise the retries will lock it again within minutes and you will be back where you
started.

Repeated failed logons from unexpected sources go to the security team before you unlock. Deliberate
administrative locks should be queried with whoever set them.
